entry.title: Why Does an LLM Take So Long to Say the First Word, Then Answer Almost Instantly?

link.title: Why Does an LLM Take So Long to Say the First Word, Then Answer Almost Instantly?

entry.content:
Paste a long document into a chatbot and hit Enter. For a moment, nothing. Then the answer pours out faster than you can read it.

Serving engineers track those two halves with separate numbers. Time to first token (TTFT) is the pause. Time per output token (TPOT) is the average gap between tokens after that (the gap between any two consecutive tokens is called inter-token latency).

The obvious guess is that the first token is expensive and the rest are cheap. The arithmetic says otherwise. Take a 70B-parameter model in FP16 on two H100 GPUs and a 4,000-token prompt (the estimate is worked out below). Prefill gets through the whole prompt in about 0.56 s, roughly 0.14 ms per token. Decode then spends about 21 ms on every single token it writes.

So per token, reading your prompt is about 150 times cheaper than writing the answer. Prefill is the efficient phase. It only feels slow because you sit through all 4,000 tokens of it before the model can say anything, while decode just has to stay ahead of your eyes. At 21 ms a token, it does.

Same weights, very different shapes

Both phases run the exact same weights. What differs is the shape of the work they hand the GPU.

In prefill, all \(N\) prompt tokens go in together as one matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}\), where \(d\) is the hidden size (8,192 for a Llama-style 70B). Each linear layer multiplies that whole matrix by a weight matrix like \(W_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\). One weight matrix, \(N\) rows of input. That’s a matrix-matrix multiply, or GEMM.

Decode feeds in a single row, \(x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times d}\), for the one new token. Same weight matrix, one row of input, so now it’s a matrix-vector multiply (GEMV).

Attention splits the same way. Every layer computes

\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

with \(Q = XW_Q\), \(K = XW_K\) and \(V = XW_V\) the query, key and value projections and \(d_k\) the size of one attention head. \(QK^\top\) is an \(N \times N\) grid of scores, one for every pair of tokens. Causal masking throws away the upper half, since a token can look back but never ahead, and prefill fills in the whole remaining triangle in a single pass.

Decode only ever needs the newest row of that triangle, and the KV cache is why. Under causal masking, a token’s key and value are fixed the moment they’re computed, because nothing that comes later can change them. So the model keeps \(K\) and \(V\) for every token it has seen. At step \(t\) it computes \(q_t\), \(k_t\) and \(v_t\) for the new token alone, appends \(k_t\) and \(v_t\) to the cache, and attends with one query:

\[o_t = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{q_t K_{1:t}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V_{1:t}\]

\(K_{1:t}\) and \(V_{1:t}\) are the cached keys and values for tokens \(1\) through \(t\), and \(o_t\) is the new token’s attention output.

  Prefill (first token) Decode (every later token)
Input per step all \(N\) prompt tokens 1 new token
Linear algebra matrix × matrix (GEMM) matrix × vector (GEMV)
Attention per layer the full \(N \times N\) triangle one row of length \(t\)
Bottleneck compute (FLOP/s) memory bandwidth (bytes/s)
What the user feels TTFT TPOT

Most of that table falls straight out of the shapes. The bottleneck row doesn’t, and it’s the row that matters. Getting to it takes two steps: count the work, then look at what actually limits the GPU.

Count the FLOPs first

A rule of thumb that holds up well is 2 FLOPs per parameter per token. Each weight does one multiply and one add for every token that passes through it. For a model with \(P\) parameters,

\[\begin{gathered} \text{FLOPs}_{\text{prefill}} \approx 2PN \\ \text{FLOPs}_{\text{decode}} \approx 2P \ \text{per token} \end{gathered}\]

Attention adds its own work on top, and that part grows with the square of the prompt length. With \(L\) layers and causal masking it’s roughly

\[\text{FLOPs}_{\text{attention}} \approx 2N^2 d L\]

This is the term people blame when they say prefill is slow “because attention is quadratic.” At ordinary prompt lengths it barely registers. For a 70B model (\(d = 8{,}192\), \(L = 80\)) at \(N = 4{,}000\), attention comes to about \(2.1 \times 10^{13}\) FLOPs against \(5.6 \times 10^{14}\) for the linear layers. Under 4%. The two only meet at

\[N^* \approx \frac{P}{dL}\]

which works out to roughly 107,000 tokens for this model, or about 53,000 if the kernel computes the masked half anyway. Below that, and once the prompt is longer than a few hundred tokens (the next section explains that threshold), prefill time grows almost linearly with prompt length, and most of it goes into the same weight matrices decode uses.

So prefill does about \(N\) times the work of a decode step, which here means 4,000 times. If FLOPs told the whole story, a decode step would take \(0.56\ \text{s} / 4{,}000 = 0.14\) ms and a 500-token answer would show up in 70 ms. Real decode is about 150 times slower than that. Arithmetic isn’t what sets its pace.

Why less math doesn’t mean less time

A GPU can run short of two things: compute, or the bandwidth to keep that compute fed. The roofline model (Williams, Waterman & Patterson, 2009) puts both limits on one chart, and once you’ve seen it, the prefill/decode split stops being mysterious.

On the x-axis sits arithmetic intensity, the math a computation does per byte it pulls from GPU memory (HBM) into the cores:

\[\text{AI} = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}}\]

The y-axis is the FLOP/s you actually get, and two ceilings cap it. At low intensity the cores mostly wait for data, so you get bandwidth × AI. That’s the sloped memory roof, and an H100 (the SXM version, which all the numbers here assume) moves 3.35 TB/s. At high intensity the cores stay busy and performance flattens out at peak, about 989 TFLOP/s of dense FP16 on an H100. (NVIDIA advertises 1,979, but that’s a with-sparsity number.) The slope meets the flat roof at the ridge point:

\[\begin{aligned} \text{AI}_{\text{ridge}} &= \frac{\text{peak FLOP/s}}{\text{bandwidth}} \\ &\approx \frac{989 \times 10^{12}}{3.35 \times 10^{12}} \approx 295 \ \text{FLOP/byte} \end{aligned}\]

Anything left of the ridge is memory-bound, anything right of it compute-bound. To see where the two phases land, remember that an FP16 weight is 2 bytes and contributes 2 FLOPs for every token it touches.

Decode reads every weight to process one token: \(2P\) FLOPs over \(2P\) bytes, so \(\text{AI} \approx 1\) FLOP/byte. Nowhere near the ridge. Each step goes on streaming 140 GB of weights while the tensor cores use well under 1% of what they could do. (Decode also re-reads the KV cache every step, which adds bytes as the context grows; I leave it out to keep the numbers simple, and it only pushes decode further left.)

Prefill reads each weight once and reuses it across all \(N\) tokens: \(2PN\) FLOPs over roughly \(2P\) bytes, so \(\text{AI} \approx N\). A few hundred tokens into the prompt it crosses the ridge, and from there the tensor cores run flat out.

Prefill takes visible time because there’s a lot of math, but it does that math at full speed. Decode has almost nothing to compute and still waits, every single step, for the whole model to come out of memory.

This is also why providers batch. If \(B\) users decode together, one pass over the weights serves all of them: \(2PB\) FLOPs over \(2P\) bytes, so \(\text{AI} \approx B\). A batch of 64 gets 64 tokens for the weight traffic of one (each user’s KV cache is still read separately). Your own tokens don’t come any faster, but the GPU does far more useful work per byte, and the compute still sitting idle turns out to be handy for prefill (more on that at the end).

The back-of-envelope version

A 70B model in FP16 is 140 GB of weights. One H100 has 80 GB. So I split the model across two GPUs with tensor parallelism, each holding half of every layer, and assume compute and bandwidth simply double, ignoring communication between the GPUs and letting real kernels reach about half of peak. That puts effective compute \(F_{\text{eff}}\) at about 500 TFLOP/s per H100, so about 1,000 TFLOP/s for the pair, and memory bandwidth \(BW\) at 3.35 TB/s each, 6.7 TB/s together.

Prefill is compute-bound, so its time is FLOPs over compute:

\[\begin{aligned} \text{TTFT} &\approx \frac{2PN}{F_{\text{eff}}} \\ &= \frac{2 \times (70 \times 10^9) \times 4{,}000}{10^{15}} \approx 0.56 \ \text{s} \end{aligned}\]

Decode is memory-bound, so its time is bytes over bandwidth:

\[\begin{aligned} \text{TPOT} &\approx \frac{\text{weight bytes}}{BW} = \frac{140 \times 10^9}{6.7 \times 10^{12}} \\ &\approx 21 \ \text{ms} \quad (\approx 48 \ \text{tokens/s}) \end{aligned}\]

Now go per token. Prefill spends \(2P / F_{\text{eff}}\) on each prompt token and decode spends \(2P / BW\) on each output token, so

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\text{decode time per token}}{\text{prefill time per token}} &= \frac{2P / BW}{2P / F_{\text{eff}}} \\ &= \frac{F_{\text{eff}}}{BW} \approx \frac{10^{15}}{6.7 \times 10^{12}} \approx 150 \end{aligned}\]

The parameter count cancels, which to me is the nicest part of the whole calculation. What’s left, the 150× gap, is the GPU’s effective ridge point: how many FLOPs it can do in the time it takes to move one byte. Run an 8B model on one H100, or a 405B model across as many H100s as it takes to hold it, and the per-token ratio stays roughly the same. Only the absolute times change. (Roughly, because attention and KV-cache traffic don’t scale with the parameter count, and small models don’t always keep the GPU busy.)

And 48 tokens a second is roughly 35 words a second, at about three-quarters of an English word per token. A typical adult reads around 4. Once prefill is done the stream outruns you, so it looks instant, even though every token in it is the expensive kind.

Why it’s even slower in a real product

That 0.56 s is a floor. A real service piles more on top, in three ways.

Start with reasoning models. They decode a hidden chain of thought before the visible answer, and those tokens run at decode speed, so the wait you actually see is

\[\begin{aligned} \text{TTFT}_{\text{visible}} &= \text{TTFT}_{\text{prefill}} \\ &\quad + N_{\text{think}} \times \text{TPOT} \end{aligned}\]

At 21 ms per token, 1,500 thinking tokens add about 31 s. Prefill is a rounding error next to that.

Then there’s the queue. A server runs many users at once, and a 10,000-token prefill done in one go would stall everyone else’s stream for as long as it runs. Schedulers like Sarathi-Serve chop long prompts into chunks and run each chunk alongside the ongoing decode batch, soaking up the idle compute the roofline says is there. Everyone keeps streaming. Your prefill, though, is now spread over several passes, and you may wait for GPU memory before it starts at all.

Last comes prefix caching, or rather missing it. If the start of your prompt (a system prompt, earlier turns in the chat) matches something the server processed recently, engines like vLLM (automatic prefix caching) and SGLang (RadixAttention) reuse its cached K and V and only prefill the new part. The catch is that every token’s K and V depend on everything before it. Change one early token, say a timestamp at the top of the system prompt, and the cache is invalid for everything after it.

Put together, the first word waits on one compute-bound pass over your whole prompt, plus whatever the service stacks in front of it. Every word after that waits on a memory-bound sweep through the weights. Per token, the first wait is still the cheap one, by about 150×.

Further reading

  • Pope et al., 2022, “Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference”, the standard analysis of prefill vs decode cost at scale, including batch size and how to split a model across chips.
  • kipply, 2022, “Transformer Inference Arithmetic”, which works the 2-FLOPs-per-parameter rule and memory- vs compute-bound decoding through by hand.
  • Yuan et al., 2024, “LLM Inference Unveiled: Survey and Roofline Model Insights”, a survey that looks at inference techniques through the roofline model.
  • Williams, Waterman & Patterson, 2009, “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures”, the original roofline paper (Communications of the ACM 52(4)).
  • Agrawal et al., 2024, “Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve”, for chunked prefill and stall-free scheduling in detail.
entry.summary: Why an LLM pauses before its first word and then streams the rest, worked through with FLOP counts, the roofline model and a 70B-on-H100 estimate.

entry.title: Why the “Correct” Setting Makes Worse Images: The Strange Math of Classifier-Free Guidance

link.title: Why the “Correct” Setting Makes Worse Images: The Strange Math of Classifier-Free Guidance

entry.content:
The paradox: the “correct” sampler makes worse images

Most Stable Diffusion interfaces have a slider for guidance, whether it’s called guidance scale, CFG scale or guidance_scale. Set it to 1 and the model does exactly what it was trained to do: it samples from \(p(x \mid c)\), the distribution of training images that match the prompt \(c\). The pictures are usually disappointing. Ask for a golden retriever and you get muddy colour and a dog-shaped blob. Move the slider to 7.5, the default in diffusers, and the same weights, starting from the same noise, give you a crisp dog you’d recognise anywhere. Push it to 20 and the image deep-fries, with neon saturation and anatomy bent the wrong way.

So the setting that is mathematically correct gives the worst pictures, and the best pictures come from a setting that is, strictly speaking, wrong. I wanted to know why, and the answer is more interesting than “guidance sharpens the distribution”.

Part of it is the data. \(p(x\mid c)\) is the distribution of web data, and captions like “a golden retriever in a park” are attached to a huge number of photos: blurry ones, badly lit ones, cropped ones, ones that barely match their caption. A faithful sampler has to reproduce all of them in proportion. That’s what covering a distribution means. Nobody judges a generated image by how typical it is of the training set, though. We judge it by how clearly it shows what we asked for, and that rewards a sharp prototype over a representative draw.

The other part is the network. It isn’t \(p(x\mid c)\); it’s an approximation, and it’s least accurate where the data is thinnest, in the gaps between modes. At \(w=1\) those errors leak into samples as washed-out textures and geometry that doesn’t hold together.

CFG fixes both by cheating. It doesn’t sample \(p(x\mid c)\), and (the part most explanations skip) it doesn’t sample the sharpened distribution it appears to target either. A better mental model is a sampler that nudges every step toward “more like the prompt than like anything else”. That one nudge helps and hurts at once. It pushes samples away from the boundaries between classes and cancels some of the network’s own error, which is good. It also overshoots the conditional mean, throws away diversity and, at large \(w\), extrapolates clean off the curved data manifold, which is bad. The sweet spot on the slider is wherever the good still outweighs the bad.

To see each effect without a trained network muddying things, I use toy models small enough that every score is exact.

Three blobs of data, one per class; the top one is the class your prompt asks for. The green shape is where guidance is supposed to send samples, and the orange dots are where it actually sends them. As the guidance weight w goes up, the green shape barely moves, but the orange dots race past it and keep going.

What classifier-free guidance is, from scratch

If you already know how a diffusion model is trained and sampled, skip ahead to the next section. This one covers the minimum the rest of the post leans on.

Diffusion in two moves

A diffusion model learns to undo noise. The forward direction is fixed and dull: take a clean image \(x_0\) and add Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\),

\[\begin{gathered} x_\sigma = x_0 + \sigma\,\epsilon, \\ \epsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, I). \end{gathered}\]

At small \(\sigma\) the image is barely touched. At large \(\sigma\) nothing of it survives, and \(x_\sigma\) is essentially pure noise. (This is the variance-exploding form, which keeps the algebra simple. Stable Diffusion 1.x uses a variance-preserving schedule that also shrinks the image as noise goes in, \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\). The two are rescalings of each other, so nothing below depends on the choice.)

The network learns the reverse direction. Given a noisy image, its noise level and the prompt, it predicts the noise that was added, \(\epsilon_\theta(x_\sigma, \sigma, c)\), trained by plain regression:

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal L &= \mathbb E_{x_0,\,c,\,\sigma,\,\epsilon} \\ &\quad \big\|\epsilon_\theta(x_0 + \sigma\epsilon,\ \sigma,\ c) - \epsilon\big\|^2 . \end{aligned}\]

A noise prediction doubles as a guess of the clean image, \(\hat x_0 = x_\sigma - \sigma\,\epsilon_\theta(x_\sigma, \sigma, c)\). It’s also a score in disguise: the best possible noise prediction is \(\epsilon^\star = -\sigma\,\nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x_\sigma \mid c)\), which is why the rest of the post can talk about scores and noise predictions interchangeably.

Sampling runs the film backwards. Start from pure noise at a large \(\sigma_{\max}\), ask the network for its noise estimate, step to a slightly smaller \(\sigma\), and repeat for a few dozen steps until \(\sigma = 0\). Each step strips out a little noise, and the prompt decides which image the noise resolves into.

Each dot is one data point, and the blue ones belong to the prompt’s class. First, noise is added until the three groups melt into a single cloud. Then the model runs the process backwards while being told the prompt, and every dot settles into the prompt’s group.

Two ways to steer toward the prompt

Feeding the prompt to the network gives you samples from \(p(x\mid c)\), which, as the paradox showed, is too non-committal. The first widely used fix was classifier guidance, popularised by Dhariwal & Nichol (2021). You train a separate classifier on noisy images, and at every sampling step you add its gradient \(\nabla_x \log p_\sigma(c \mid x)\) to nudge the sample toward images the classifier calls \(c\). It works. The catch is that it needs an extra model trained on noisy inputs, and for free-form text prompts it isn’t obvious what that classifier would even be.

Ho & Salimans (2022) got rid of the classifier. During training, the prompt is replaced by an empty prompt \(\varnothing\) some fraction of the time, so a single network learns two models at once: a conditional one, \(\epsilon_\theta(x_\sigma,\sigma,c)\), and an unconditional one, \(\epsilon_\theta(x_\sigma,\sigma,\varnothing)\). Nothing else about training changes.

Training a CFG model is ordinary diffusion training plus one coin flip: some of the time the prompt is hidden. That is how a single network learns to make predictions both with and without the prompt.

At sampling time, every step calls the network twice, once with the prompt and once with the empty prompt, and blends the two predictions with a guidance weight \(w\):

\[\begin{aligned} \tilde\epsilon &= \epsilon_\theta(x_\sigma,\sigma,\varnothing) \\ &\quad + w\,\big[\epsilon_\theta(x_\sigma,\sigma,c) - \epsilon_\theta(x_\sigma,\sigma,\varnothing)\big]. \end{aligned}\]

The guided prediction goes into whatever solver step you’d have used anyway. It costs two network evaluations per step (usually batched into one call), and that’s the whole recipe.

The geometry: a point on a line

The formula has a simple picture. For a given noisy input the two predictions are two points, and \(\tilde\epsilon\) always lies on the line through them. At \(w=0\) it sits on the unconditional prediction, at \(w=1\) on the conditional one, for \(0<w<1\) it interpolates between them, and for \(w>1\) it walks past the conditional prediction along \(\epsilon_\text{cond} - \epsilon_\text{uncond}\), the direction of “what the prompt adds”. Since \(\hat x_0 = x_\sigma - \sigma\epsilon\) is affine in \(\epsilon\), the same picture holds for the clean-image guesses: the guided guess \(\tilde x_0\) sits on the line through the unconditional and conditional guesses, at the same \(w\).

The grey and blue dots are the model’s two guesses, without and with the prompt. CFG’s final guess (orange) always sits on the line through them. Between the two dots it is a blend; beyond the blue dot, where everyday settings like 7.5 live, it is pushed further than the prompt-aware model itself would go.

The scales people actually use (7.5 is the diffusers default) are well above 1, so in practice CFG is always extrapolating, pushing past what the conditional model itself believes. The rest of the post works out what that extrapolation does to the samples.

Two arrows and a knob

A diffusion sampler starts from pure noise and keeps asking the network one question: from here, which way looks more like data? The answer is the score \(\nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x)\), the gradient of the log-density of the data after it has been blurred by Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\). Add a prompt and you ask for the conditional score \(\nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x\mid c)\) instead.

CFG asks both and compares. The unconditional arrow points toward “any natural image”, which at high noise means the blurry average of everything the noisy state could turn into. The conditional arrow points toward “an image of \(c\)”. The difference between them is the direction that makes the sample more like \(c\) compared with everything else, and CFG takes the unconditional arrow and adds \(w\) copies of that difference. That really is the whole method.

Each small arrow shows which way a noisy point gets pushed at that spot. The big arrows at the white dot show the recipe: grey (towards any image) plus w times green (towards the prompt and away from the other classes) gives orange (where CFG actually pushes). As w grows, the green part takes over and the whole field swings up and away from the other two classes.

Writing it down takes three lines. Bayes’ rule splits the conditional score into a prior term and a classifier term (\(\log p(c)\) doesn’t depend on \(x\), so it vanishes from the gradient):

\[\begin{aligned} \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x\mid c) &= \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x) \\ &\quad + \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(c\mid x). \end{aligned}\]

Rearrange it, and a conditional model plus an unconditional one hand you a classifier gradient for free. This is the implicit classifier:

\[\begin{aligned} \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(c\mid x) &= \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x\mid c) \\ &\quad - \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x). \end{aligned}\]

Classifier guidance (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021) scaled the gradient of a separately trained classifier. CFG scales the implicit one instead, by the guidance weight \(w\):

\[\begin{aligned} \tilde s_w(x,\sigma) &= \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x) \\ &\quad + w\,\big[\nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x\mid c) - \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x)\big]. \end{aligned}\]

\(w=0\) gives you the unconditional model, \(w=1\) the plain conditional one, and anything with \(w>1\) is guidance. In practice networks predict noise rather than scores, but for the variance-exploding process \(x_\sigma = x_0 + \sigma\epsilon\) I use throughout, the two differ only by a factor, \(\hat\epsilon = -\sigma\,\nabla_x\log p_\sigma(x)\), so the same rule becomes

\[\tilde\epsilon = \epsilon_\text{uncond} + w\,(\epsilon_\text{cond} - \epsilon_\text{uncond}),\]

which you’ll find, almost word for word, inside the Stable Diffusion pipelines in diffusers. Both predictions come from the same network, trained with the prompt-dropout trick from the primer above (Ho & Salimans, 2022). Watch the notation if you read that paper. Ho & Salimans write \((1+w')\,\epsilon_\text{cond} - w'\,\epsilon_\text{uncond}\), so their \(w'\) is our \(w-1\). I stick to the diffusers convention, where guidance_scale = 1 means no guidance at all (diffusers only turns CFG on when guidance_scale > 1).

One step of sampling with CFG: run the network twice, combine the two answers using the guidance weight, take a small denoising step, and repeat. The combine step is where both the benefits and the side effects of guidance come from.

A toy where every score is exact

I don’t want a trained network sitting between us and the formula. So the toy has to be something whose scores can be written down exactly. Mine is a mixture of three 2D Gaussians at 90°, 210° and 330° on the unit circle, each with standard deviation 0.5, one per “class”, and the prompt \(c\) picks the top one. Adding noise of level \(\sigma\) to a Gaussian mixture just widens each component’s variance by \(\sigma^2\), so \(p_\sigma(x)\), \(p_\sigma(x\mid c)\) and both scores stay closed-form at every noise level. Cell 1 pins the two dependencies and gives each role a colour that every figure reuses: grey for the unconditional model, blue for the conditional one, green for the tilted target (coming up shortly), orange for CFG and violet for autoguidance.

%pip install -q "numpy==2.3.3" "matplotlib==3.10.8"
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap

SEED = 0
np.random.seed(SEED)

# One colour per *role*, used the same way in every figure of the post.
COL = {"uncond": "#52514e", "cond": "#2a78d6", "cfg": "#eb6834", "target": "#1baf7a", "auto": "#6250d6"}
TARGET_CMAP = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("target", ["#fcfcfb", COL["target"]])
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 110, "figure.facecolor": "#fcfcfb", "axes.facecolor": "#fcfcfb",
    "axes.edgecolor": "#c3c2b7", "axes.labelcolor": "#0b0b0b", "text.color": "#0b0b0b",
    "xtick.color": "#52514e", "ytick.color": "#52514e", "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": "#e8e7e3",
    "grid.linewidth": 0.6, "lines.linewidth": 2, "font.size": 10,
})
print(f"numpy {np.__version__} | matplotlib {matplotlib.__version__} | seed {SEED}")

numpy 2.3.3 | matplotlib 3.10.8 | seed 0

Cell 2 builds the scores and checks the algebra before anything leans on it. mixture_score computes \(\nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x)\) for any mixture, score_uncond and score_cond are the two models, and cfg_score(w) returns \(\tilde s_w\). The first check compares the implicit classifier with the gradient of the true classifier \(\log p_\sigma(c\mid x)\), which the cell gets independently by finite differences. The second confirms that the noise form and the score form of CFG really are one formula. Then it draws the arrows at a single noisy point.

MEANS = np.stack([np.cos(np.deg2rad([90, 210, 330])), np.sin(np.deg2rad([90, 210, 330]))], axis=1)
VARS, UNIFORM, PROMPT = np.full(3, 0.5**2), np.full(3, 1 / 3), 0   # 3 classes; the prompt picks the top one
PROMPT_DIR = MEANS[PROMPT]                                         # unit vector toward the prompt's mode

def logsumexp(a: np.ndarray, axis: int) -> np.ndarray:
    m = a.max(axis, keepdims=True)
    return (m + np.log(np.exp(a - m).sum(axis, keepdims=True))).squeeze(axis)

def component_logits(x: np.ndarray, sigma: float, means: np.ndarray, vars_: np.ndarray, weights: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """log w_k N(x; m_k, (v_k + sigma^2) I): VE noising just widens every component by sigma^2."""
    v = vars_[None, :] + sigma**2
    return np.log(weights)[None] - 0.5 * ((x[:, None] - means[None]) ** 2).sum(-1) / v - np.log(2 * np.pi * v)

def log_density(x, sigma, means, vars_, weights) -> np.ndarray:
    return logsumexp(component_logits(x, sigma, means, vars_, weights), axis=1)

def mixture_score(x, sigma, means, vars_, weights) -> np.ndarray:
    """Exact grad_x log p_sigma(x): responsibility-weighted pull toward each component mean."""
    logits = component_logits(x, sigma, means, vars_, weights)
    resp = np.exp(logits - logsumexp(logits, axis=1)[:, None])
    return -(resp[..., None] * (x[:, None] - means[None]) / (vars_[None, :, None] + sigma**2)).sum(1)

def score_uncond(x, s): return mixture_score(x, s, MEANS, VARS, UNIFORM)
def score_cond(x, s): return mixture_score(x, s, MEANS[[PROMPT]], VARS[[PROMPT]], np.ones(1))

def cfg_score(w: float, cond=score_cond, uncond=score_uncond):

The distribution CFG seems to aim for

The usual reading of the formula goes like this. If \(\tilde s_w\) were the score of a single distribution, that distribution would be

\[\begin{aligned} \tilde p_w(x\mid c) &\propto p(x)\,p(c\mid x)^{w} \\ &\propto p(x)^{1-w}\,p(x\mid c)^{w}, \end{aligned}\]

where the second form uses \(p(c\mid x) = p(x\mid c)\,p(c)/p(x)\). Raising the classifier to the power \(w\) is like telling the model to be \(w\) times as picky about the prompt. Points the classifier is sure about keep their density. Ambiguous points near a decision boundary, where \(p(c\mid x)\) hovers around a half, get crushed by the extra factor \(p(c\mid x)^{w-1}\). Picture the prompt’s mode shrinking and edging away from its neighbours. I’ll call \(\tilde p_w\) the tilted target.

It’s a tidy story, and the next section shows it’s wrong, because sampling with \(\tilde s_w\) doesn’t produce this distribution. The target is still worth drawing, since everything later gets measured against it. Cell 3 evaluates \(p(x)^{1-w}p(x\mid c)^w\) on clean data (\(\sigma=0\)) over an 80 × 80 grid for \(w \in \{1, 3, 6, 15\}\), and reports where the target sits along the prompt’s axis, how wide it is, and how much of its mass lies where the true classifier is less than 90% sure (\(p(c\mid x) < 0.9\)).

Why CFG never gets there

A diffusion sampler doesn’t follow the score of one distribution. It follows a whole family of scores, one per noise level, and it only ends up sampling \(q\) if every member of that family is the score of \(q\) blurred to that level. Blurring and sharpening don’t commute, though. Sharpen and then blur, or blur and then sharpen, and you get two different densities. CFG builds its scores the second way.

The same two operations done in two different orders. Top route: sharpen first, then blur, which is what a correct sampler would need. Left and bottom route: blur first, then sharpen, which is what CFG actually does. The green and orange curves at the end don’t match, and that mismatch is why CFG can’t land on the target it seems to aim for.

To make that precise, write \(\mathcal N_\sigma *\) for convolution with \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2 I)\), which is what the forward process does to a density. A valid reverse process for the tilted target needs the scores of \(\mathcal N_\sigma * \tilde p_w\). CFG doesn’t give it those. It gives it the score of the tilted noisy marginals, and in general

\[\begin{gathered} \mathcal N_\sigma * \big(p_0^{1-w}\,p_0(\cdot\mid c)^{w}\big) \\ \not\propto\; p_\sigma^{1-w}\,p_\sigma(\cdot\mid c)^{w}. \end{gathered}\]

So the CFG scores at different noise levels aren’t the noisy versions of any one clean distribution. The sampler is chasing a target that keeps moving as \(\sigma\) shrinks. Two 1D Gaussians show what that does.

Case A, equal variances. Take \(p_0(x)=\mathcal N(0,s_0^2)\) and \(p_0(x\mid c)=\mathcal N(\mu,s_0^2)\). Noise keeps both Gaussian with variance \(v_\sigma=s_0^2+\sigma^2\), and the CFG score collapses into the score of a single Gaussian:

\[\begin{aligned} \tilde s_w(x,\sigma) &= (1-w)\,\frac{-x}{v_\sigma} + w\,\frac{-(x-\mu)}{v_\sigma} \\ &= -\frac{x - w\mu}{v_\sigma}. \end{aligned}\]

That’s exactly the score of \(\mathcal N(w\mu,\ s_0^2+\sigma^2)\) at every \(\sigma\), a perfectly valid family, so CFG samples \(\mathcal N(w\mu, s_0^2)\). Here blurring and tilting happen to commute (the tilt is a pure shift), so CFG does land on the tilted target. Look at where that target is, though. The mean has moved from \(\mu\) to \(w\mu\), so CFG overshoots the conditional mean, linearly in \(w\). For images, whatever separates “red apple” from “apple” gets multiplied by \(w\), and out comes a neon apple.

A one-dimensional example. Blue is the true distribution for the prompt and orange is what CFG produces. The orange curve keeps the same width, but its centre slides to w times the true centre, so at w = 6 it sits at 6 instead of 1.

Case B, unequal variances. Now centre both at zero and make the conditional narrower: \(p_0(x)=\mathcal N(0,\sigma_u^2)\) and \(p_0(x\mid c)=\mathcal N(0,\sigma_c^2)\) with \(\sigma_c<\sigma_u\). The CFG score is linear, \(\tilde s_w = -\tilde\tau_\sigma\,x\), with precision

\[\tilde\tau_\sigma = \frac{w}{\sigma_c^2+\sigma^2} - \frac{w-1}{\sigma_u^2+\sigma^2}.\]

Any Gaussian that has been through the forward process has precision \(1/(a+\sigma^2)\) for some fixed clean variance \(a\). Put differently, the implied clean variance \(1/\tilde\tau_\sigma - \sigma^2\) has to be the same at every \(\sigma\). For CFG it isn’t. At \(\sigma=0\) it matches the tilted target’s variance \(\big(w/\sigma_c^2-(w-1)/\sigma_u^2\big)^{-1}\), and as \(\sigma\to\infty\) it heads to \(w\sigma_c^2-(w-1)\sigma_u^2\), which goes negative whenever \(w\sigma_c^2 < (w-1)\sigma_u^2\). (You’ll sometimes read that \(\tilde\tau_\sigma\) blows up as \(\sigma\to0\). It doesn’t; it’s finite there. What breaks is its shape across noise levels.)

The ODE is linear, so it integrates in closed form. Start at \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\max}^2)\), run down to \(\sigma=0\), take the limit \(\sigma_{\max}\to\infty\), and the samples end up with standard deviation

\[\text{std}_\text{ODE} = \frac{\sigma_c^{\,w}}{\sigma_u^{\,w-1}},\]

which is not the tilted target’s \(\big(w/\sigma_c^2-(w-1)/\sigma_u^2\big)^{-1/2}\).

Bradley & Nakkiran (2024) prove the general version: neither DDPM nor DDIM sampling with CFG produces the “gamma-powered” distribution \(p(x)^{1-w}p(x\mid c)^{w}\), and the two samplers don’t even agree with each other. They also say what CFG is instead. In the SDE limit it’s a predictor-corrector method in the sense of Song et al. (2020), alternating a DDIM-style denoising step on the conditional distribution with a Langevin correction that sharpens toward a gamma-powered distribution at the current noise level. If you want one line for what the guidance slider does, “denoise, then sharpen, then repeat” is the most honest one I know.

Two counterexamples you can run

Cell 4 adds the sampler that the rest of the post reuses. sample runs the reverse variance-exploding process from \(\mathcal N(0, 80^2)\) down to \(\sigma=0\) on the noise schedule from Karras et al. (2022), and it can do that three ways. ode integrates the probability-flow ODE \(dx/d\sigma = -\sigma\,\tilde s_w(x,\sigma)\) with Heun’s method. ddim uses plain Euler on the same ODE, which in this parameterisation is exactly DDIM with \(\eta=0\). sde runs the reverse SDE and adds fresh Gaussian noise at every step. The cell then samples Case A at \(w=3\) (\(s_0=0.5\), \(\mu=1\)) and Case B at \(w\in\{1,3,6\}\) (\(\sigma_c=0.5\), \(\sigma_u=1\)), and plots the implied clean variance against \(\sigma\).

def karras_sigmas(steps: int, s_min: float = 0.002, s_max: float = 80.0, rho: float = 7.0) -> np.ndarray:
    ramp = np.linspace(0, 1, steps)
    return np.append((s_max ** (1 / rho) + ramp * (s_min ** (1 / rho) - s_max ** (1 / rho))) ** rho, 0.0)

def sample(score_fn, n: int, dim: int, steps: int = 40, method: str = "ode", seed: int = SEED) -> np.ndarray:
    """Reverse VE diffusion from N(0, s_max^2 I).
    ode  = Heun on the probability-flow ODE dx/dsigma = -sigma * score
    ddim = Euler on the same ODE (exactly DDIM with eta = 0 in VE form)
    sde  = reverse SDE, Euler-Maruyama: fresh Gaussian noise every step."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    sig = karras_sigmas(steps)
    x = sig[0] * rng.standard_normal((n, dim))
    for s, s_next in zip(sig[:-1], sig[1:]):
        if method == "sde":
            g2 = s**2 - s_next**2
            x = x + g2 * score_fn(x, s) + np.sqrt(g2) * rng.standard_normal(x.shape)
            continue
        d = -s * score_fn(x, s)
        x_next = x + (s_next - s) * d
        if method == "ode" and s_next > 0:                       # Heun correction
            x_next = x + (s_next - s) * 0.5 * (d - s_next * score_fn(x_next, s_next))
        x = x_next
    return x

In 2D, samples run from the boundaries

Back in 2D both cases happen at once, and the mixture adds a third effect of its own. Near the origin all three modes overlap, so the unconditional density \(p_\sigma(x)\) is high there. The CFG score contains a \(-(w-1)\,\nabla_x\log p_\sigma(x)\) term, so whenever \(w>1\) it actively climbs down the unconditional density. Wherever classes overlap, guidance shoves samples out of the overlap and through the far side of the prompt’s mode. The cloud overshoots the mode centre and piles up on its outer rim, about as far from the other classes as it can get. Chidambaram et al. (2024) prove a version of this for mixtures of Gaussians and of compactly supported distributions: as guidance grows, samples increasingly favour the boundary of the conditional’s support.

That one picture holds both the help and the harm. Being far from the decision boundary is what makes a sample unambiguous, a golden retriever nobody would mistake for a cat. Sitting on the far rim of the mode is what makes it exaggerated, a retriever that’s somehow extra golden.

N_SAMPLES = 8000

def kl_to_grid(samples: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Histogram estimate of KL(samples || q) on the shared grid (q holds bin masses)."""
    h, _, _ = np.histogram2d(samples[:, 0], samples[:, 1], bins=[EDGES, EDGES])
    p = h.ravel() / len(samples)
    m = p > 0
    return float((p[m] * np.log(p[m] / np.maximum(q[m], 1e-300))).sum())

def draw_from_grid(q: np.ndarray, n: int, seed: int = SEED) -> np.ndarray:
    """Exact samples from the grid distribution q: the estimator's noise floor."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    cell = EDGES[1] - EDGES[0]
    return GRID[rng.choice(len(q), size=n, p=q)] + rng.uniform(-cell / 2, cell / 2, (n, 2))

Why the SDE sampler does better

Case B already showed the SDE sampler ending up much closer to the tilted target than the ODE. The difference comes down to what each one does with an error. A deterministic sampler commits to its trajectory, so whatever mismatch it picks up at high noise between the CFG scores and any valid family, it carries all the way to the end. A stochastic sampler injects fresh noise at every step and then partly removes it. That loop behaves like Langevin dynamics, and Langevin dynamics driven by \(\tilde s_w\) pulls samples toward the distribution whose score \(\tilde s_w\) actually is at the current noise level, \(p_\sigma(x)^{1-w}\,p_\sigma(x\mid c)^{w}\). Step after step, the SDE re-equilibrates toward that moving density, so it finishes nearer the tilted target. That’s the corrector in Bradley & Nakkiran’s picture.

There’s a practical consequence. The same guidance_scale does different things under a deterministic solver (DDIM, DPM-Solver-style ODE samplers) and a stochastic one (ancestral or DDPM-style), so a setting you tuned for one sampler won’t carry over one-to-one to the other.

Same model, same w = 6, same starting points, two ways of running the sampler. The smooth version (left) overshoots the green target. The noisy version (right) keeps getting nudged back and finishes much closer to it.

One guidance weight, three samplers

Cell 6 fixes \(w=6\) and runs all three samplers from the same seed, with exact draws from the target as a reference row.

w = 6
q = tilted_target(w)
runs = {
    "ODE  (Heun, 40 steps)": sample(cfg_score(w), N_SAMPLES, 2, steps=40, method="ode"),
    "DDIM (Euler, 25 steps)": sample(cfg_score(w), N_SAMPLES, 2, steps=25, method="ddim"),
    "SDE  (Euler-Maruyama, 250 steps)": sample(cfg_score(w), N_SAMPLES, 2, steps=250, method="sde"),
    "exact draws from the target": draw_from_grid(q, N_SAMPLES),
}
print(f"w = {w}: KL to the tilted target p(x)^(1-w) p(x|c)^w   [target mean along prompt axis {q @ GRID @ PROMPT_DIR:.2f}]")
for name, xs in runs.items():
    print(f"  {name:<34} KL {kl_to_grid(xs, q):5.2f} | mean along prompt axis {(xs @ PROMPT_DIR).mean():.2f}")

w = 6: KL to the tilted target p(x)^(1-w) p(x|c)^w   [target mean along prompt axis 1.18]
  ODE  (Heun, 40 steps)              KL  2.77 | mean along prompt axis 2.15
  DDIM (Euler, 25 steps)             KL  3.31 | mean along prompt axis 2.20
  SDE  (Euler-Maruyama, 250 steps)   KL  0.40 | mean along prompt axis 1.52
  exact draws from the target        KL  0.04 | mean along prompt axis 1.18

The disagreement is large. With identical scores and the same \(w\), the ODE ends at KL 2.77 and DDIM at 3.31, while the SDE reaches 0.40 against a floor of 0.04. The means say the same thing: the target sits at 1.18 along the prompt’s axis, the SDE at 1.52, the ODE at 2.15 and DDIM at 2.20. Noise doesn’t fix CFG, and 0.40 is still ten times the floor. It does cut the KL by about a factor of seven (2.77 to 0.40) and the mean overshoot by about a factor of three (0.97 to 0.34), which is what you’d expect if the injected noise is doing correction work the deterministic samplers never get to do.

Looking at the clean image instead

Everything so far happened in noisy space. To see what CFG does to images, it helps to look at the network’s guess of the clean image instead. Tweedie’s formula (Efron, 2011) ties the score to the best possible denoiser, the posterior mean of the clean image given the noisy one:

\[\begin{aligned} \hat x_0(x_\sigma) &= \mathbb E[x_0\mid x_\sigma] \\ &= x_\sigma + \sigma^2\,\nabla_x\log p_\sigma(x_\sigma). \end{aligned}\]

Plug in the CFG score and the \(x_\sigma\) terms cancel:

\[\begin{aligned} \tilde x_0 &= \hat x_0(x_\sigma) \\ &\quad + w\,\big[\hat x_0(x_\sigma, c) - \hat x_0(x_\sigma)\big]. \end{aligned}\]

In clean-image space, then, CFG draws a straight line from the unconditional guess through the conditional guess, and keeps going for another \(w-1\) times that distance.

That line is why guidance helps. At high and medium noise \(\hat x_0\) is a mean, the average of every clean image the noisy state could have come from. Natural images live on a thin, curved manifold, and the average of points on a curve sits inside the curve, off the manifold. That’s the blur in a \(w=1\) sample’s early steps. The difference vector \(\hat x_0(x_\sigma,c) - \hat x_0(x_\sigma)\) points from the global average toward the prompt’s average. Part of it is normal to the prompt’s patch of the manifold and pulls the guess back onto it; part of it is tangent and pushes the guess away from neighbouring classes.

It’s also why guidance hurts. The manifold curves and the line doesn’t, so once the line has crossed the manifold, more \(w\) only carries it further out, into high-norm territory where the implicit classifier is extremely confident and no real image lives. In pixel space that’s the deep-fried look: saturated colour as pixel norms grow, plus exaggerated edges. Chidambaram et al. (2024) arrive at the same place from the other side. With any nonzero score error, a large enough guidance weight pushes samples off the support of the data.

The circle stands for the set of real images, and the blue half is what the prompt asks for. CFG builds its guess (orange) by extending a straight line from the ‘any image’ guess through the ‘prompt’ guess. A little guidance puts the guess right on the circle; more guidance shoots it straight past, into territory where no real image exists. That is the deep-fried look.

Off-manifold behaviour is exactly what CFG++ (Chung et al., 2024) targets. Its authors blame CFG’s off-manifold behaviour for mode collapse, and they reformulate the guided step so it stays on the manifold.

A circle for a manifold

Cell 7 swaps the three blobs for something curved: the unit circle, built from 128 narrow Gaussians (std 0.03), with the prompt picking the upper half. It draws 4,000 noisy points from the prompt’s half at \(\sigma=1\), computes both Tweedie denoisers exactly, and checks that score-space CFG and \(\hat x_0\)-space extrapolation really are the same operation. Then it turns up \(w\) and tracks two things: how far \(\tilde x_0\) lands off the circle (the harm), and how deep it sits inside the prompt’s half, measured as the mean of \(\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle of \(\tilde x_0\) around the circle (the help; 1 is the top of the circle and 0 is the class boundary).

K, RING_STD = 128, 0.03
theta = (np.arange(K) + 0.5) * 2 * np.pi / K
RING = np.stack([np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)], axis=1)       # data manifold: the unit circle
UPPER = RING[:, 1] > 0                                         # the prompt selects the upper half

def ring_score(x, s, mask): return mixture_score(x, s, RING[mask], np.full(mask.sum(), RING_STD**2), np.full(mask.sum(), 1 / mask.sum()))
def denoiser(x, s, mask): return x + s**2 * ring_score(x, s, mask)   # Tweedie: E[x0 | x_t]

sigma, rng = 1.0, np.random.default_rng(SEED)
xt = RING[UPPER][rng.integers(0, UPPER.sum(), 4000)] + RING_STD * rng.standard_normal((4000, 2)) + sigma * rng.standard_normal((4000, 2))
x0_u, x0_c = denoiser(xt, sigma, np.ones(K, bool)), denoiser(xt, sigma, UPPER)
via_score = xt + sigma**2 * cfg_score(4.0, lambda x, s: ring_score(x, s, UPPER), lambda x, s: ring_score(x, s, np.ones(K, bool)))(xt, sigma)
print(f"Tweedie check, w=4: CFG in score space vs extrapolation in x0-hat space, max |diff| = {np.abs(via_score - (x0_u + 4.0 * (x0_c - x0_u))).max():.1e}")

ws = np.concatenate([np.linspace(1, 3, 9), [4, 5, 6, 7.5, 10, 15, 20]])
extrap = {w: x0_u + w * (x0_c - x0_u) for w in ws}
off = np.array([np.abs(np.linalg.norm(extrap[w], axis=1) - 1).mean() for w in ws])            # harm: distance off the circle
margin = np.array([(extrap[w][:, 1] / np.linalg.norm(extrap[w], axis=1)).mean() for w in ws])  # help: depth into the class (sin of angle)
for w in [1, 1.5, 2, 3, 7.5, 20]:
    i = int(np.argmin(np.abs(ws - w)))
    print(f"  w={w:>4}: off-manifold distance {off[i]:.3f} | class margin {margin[i]:.3f}")
print(f"off-manifold distance is smallest at w = {ws[off.argmin()]:g} (sigma = {sigma})")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.9))
t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400)
axes[0].plot(np.cos(t), np.sin(t), color=COL["uncond"], linewidth=1)
axes[0].plot(np.cos(t[t < np.pi]), np.sin(t[t < np.pi]), color=COL["cond"], linewidth=3, label="prompt's sub-manifold")
for w, c in [(1, "#f5b393"), (1.5, COL["cfg"]), (3, "#a8401a")]:              # light -> dark = more guidance
    axes[0].scatter(*extrap[w][:250].T, s=6, color=c, alpha=0.7, linewidths=0, label=f"$\\tilde x_0$, w = {w:g}")
axes[0].set_aspect("equal"); axes[0].set_xlim(-2.6, 2.6); axes[0].set_ylim(-1.3, 2.8)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper left", markerscale=2.5); axes[0].set_title(f"Extrapolated $\\tilde x_0$ at $\\sigma$ = {sigma}")
axes[1].plot(ws, margin, color=COL["cond"]); axes[1].set_xlabel("guidance w"); axes[1].set_ylabel("mean sin(angle)")
axes[1].set_title("Help: depth into the class (saturates)")
axes[2].plot(ws, off, color=COL["cfg"]); axes[2].set_xlabel("guidance w"); axes[2].set_ylabel("mean | ||x|| - 1 |")
axes[2].set_title("Harm: distance off the manifold")
axes[2].axvline(ws[off.argmin()], color="#0b0b0b", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
plt.show()

Tweedie check, w=4: CFG in score space vs extrapolation in x0-hat space, max |diff| = 8.9e-16
  w=   1: off-manifold distance 0.235 | class margin 0.843
  w= 1.5: off-manifold distance 0.087 | class margin 0.901
  w=   2: off-manifold distance 0.180 | class margin 0.931
  w=   3: off-manifold distance 0.538 | class margin 0.961
  w= 7.5: off-manifold distance 2.367 | class margin 0.992
  w=  20: off-manifold distance 7.560 | class margin 0.997
off-manifold distance is smallest at w = 1.5 (sigma = 1.0)

Left: CFG’s guesses for many noisy points at three guidance weights, light orange for w = 1 through dark orange for w = 3. Middle: how firmly the guesses sit inside the prompt’s half, which improves quickly and then levels off. Right: how far the guesses land from the circle, which dips at first and then climbs steadily. The dashed line marks the best setting for this toy.

The identity holds to \(8.9\times10^{-16}\), and the geometry plays out the way the argument said it would. At \(w=1\) the conditional guess is a blurry average sitting 0.235 inside the circle. A little guidance pulls it onto the manifold: at \(w=1.5\) it’s only 0.087 off, 2.7 times closer. Then the distance climbs again, close to linearly, through 0.180 at \(w=2\), 0.538 at \(w=3\) and 2.367 at \(w=7.5\), up to 7.560 at \(w=20\). The class margin shoots up early and flattens out: 0.843 at \(w=1\), 0.901 at \(w=1.5\), 0.961 at \(w=3\) and 0.997 at \(w=20\). Nearly all the help shows up early. The harm keeps coming. The optimum here, \(w=1.5\), is specific to this circle at this noise level, so don’t read anything into the value itself. What carries over is the shape, a short descent followed by a long climb.

Guidance also covers for a bad network

Everything above used exact scores, and with exact scores \(w=1\) is already perfect. There’s nothing for guidance to fix. A trained network isn’t exact, and its errors aren’t random: networks are least accurate in the low-density regions between modes, where they saw the least data. Two kinds of error matter most in practice. The model is blurry, with too much spread around each mode, and it leaks, putting some of the prompt’s probability on neighbouring classes. The leak is just imperfect prompt-following under another name.

CFG goes straight at the leak. Mass that leaked to another class sits exactly where \(p(c\mid x)\) is small, which is what guidance suppresses, so this is the error-correction half of the help. Karras et al. (2024) follow that idea to its end with autoguidance. If guidance works by extrapolating away from errors, guide the model with a deliberately worse version of itself (smaller or less trained, with the same conditioning) instead of an unconditional model. The difference vector then points away from the model’s own mistakes without also pointing away from the other classes, and you get the correction without the exaggeration. On ImageNet they report FIDs of 1.01 at 64×64 and 1.25 at 512×512.

Building a deliberately bad model

Cell 8 builds the imperfect model by hand from the same three-class mixture: every component 1.3 times too wide, with 20% of the prompt’s mass leaked onto the other two classes. The “bad” model for autoguidance gets the same treatment at 1.8 times and 40%. Autoguidance is the CFG formula unchanged, with the bad conditional model sitting where the unconditional model used to be. This time every sampler is scored against the true conditional \(p(x\mid c)\), since the question now is which one gets closest to the real thing.

def weak_model(blur: float, leak: float):
    """An imperfect network, analytically: every component too wide (blur) and part of the
    prompt's mass leaking onto the other classes (imperfect prompt-following)."""
    v = VARS * blur**2
    w_c = np.full(3, leak / 2)
    w_c[PROMPT] = 1 - leak
    return (lambda x, s: mixture_score(x, s, MEANS, v, w_c)), (lambda x, s: mixture_score(x, s, MEANS, v, UNIFORM))

main_cond, main_uncond = weak_model(blur=1.3, leak=0.2)        # the model we ship
bad_cond, _ = weak_model(blur=1.8, leak=0.4)                   # a worse version of it, for autoguidance
q_true = tilted_target(1.0)                                    # w = 1 tilt is the true conditional p(x|c)
ws = [1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8]
kl_cfg = [kl_to_grid(sample(cfg_score(w, main_cond, main_uncond), N_SAMPLES, 2), q_true) for w in ws]
kl_auto = [kl_to_grid(sample(cfg_score(w, main_cond, bad_cond), N_SAMPLES, 2), q_true) for w in ws]   # same formula, worse model in the "uncond" slot
kl_exact = kl_to_grid(sample(score_cond, N_SAMPLES, 2), q_true)

print(f"KL to the TRUE conditional p(x|c)   [exact model, w=1: {kl_exact:.2f}]")
for w, a, b in zip(ws, kl_cfg, kl_auto):
    print(f"  w={w:>3}: weak model + CFG {a:5.2f} | weak model + autoguidance {b:5.2f}")
print(f"best CFG: w={ws[int(np.argmin(kl_cfg))]} (KL {min(kl_cfg):.2f}) | best autoguidance: w={ws[int(np.argmin(kl_auto))]} (KL {min(kl_auto):.2f})")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
ax.plot(ws, kl_cfg, marker="o", color=COL["cfg"], label="weak model + CFG")
ax.plot(ws, kl_auto, marker="o", color=COL["auto"], label="weak model + autoguidance")
ax.axhline(kl_exact, color=COL["uncond"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1, label="exact model, w = 1")
ax.set_xlabel("guidance w"); ax.set_ylabel("KL to true $p(x\\mid c)$"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("Guidance as error correction: help first, then harm")
plt.show()

KL to the TRUE conditional p(x|c)   [exact model, w=1: 0.07]
  w=  1: weak model + CFG  1.15 | weak model + autoguidance  1.15
  w=1.5: weak model + CFG  0.63 | weak model + autoguidance  0.59
  w=  2: weak model + CFG  0.50 | weak model + autoguidance  0.29
  w=2.5: weak model + CFG  0.63 | weak model + autoguidance  0.23
  w=  3: weak model + CFG  0.90 | weak model + autoguidance  0.32
  w=  4: weak model + CFG  1.60 | weak model + autoguidance  0.80
  w=  6: weak model + CFG  3.18 | weak model + autoguidance  2.12
  w=  8: weak model + CFG  4.83 | weak model + autoguidance  3.31
best CFG: w=2 (KL 0.50) | best autoguidance: w=2.5 (KL 0.23)

How close each method gets to the true prompt distribution as guidance increases (lower is better). Plain CFG (orange) improves a little and then gets much worse. Autoguidance (violet) improves more before it turns around. The dashed line is what a perfect model scores.

The weak model starts at KL 1.15 at \(w=1\), where the exact model scores 0.07. A little guidance helps: CFG drops to 0.63 at \(w=1.5\) and 0.50 at \(w=2\). Then the harm takes over: 0.90 at \(w=3\), then 3.18 at \(w=6\) and 4.83 at \(w=8\), far worse than not guiding at all (1.15). Autoguidance traces the same U, only lower, and bottoms out at 0.23 at \(w=2.5\). That’s less than half of CFG’s best, because its extrapolation strips out the model’s own blur and leak without also shoving samples away from the other classes. Neither gets back to 0.07, though. Guidance can’t stand in for a better network, and here plain CFG at its best is still seven times worse than the exact model.

Where the sweet spot comes from

Line up the measurements and the one knob turns out to drive two groups of effects:

  Effect Where we measured it How it changes with \(w\)
Help Repulsion from decision boundaries cell 3: ambiguous mass 0.232 → 0.014 saturates: nothing is less ambiguous than certain
Help Pull onto the prompt’s manifold cell 7: off-manifold 0.235 → 0.087 only until the line crosses the curve
Help Cancelling the model’s leak and blur cell 8: KL 1.15 → 0.50 only until the error is cancelled
Harm Mean overshoot cells 4 and 5: 1 → \(w\mu\); 0.99 → 3.03 linear in 1D, sublinear in the 2D mixture
Harm Variance collapse, lost diversity cells 4 and 5: std 0.50 → 0.125 (1D, \(w=3\)); 0.504 → 0.284 (2D) compounds with \(w\)
Harm Extrapolation off the curved manifold cell 7: 0.087 → 7.560 grows roughly linearly

The help saturates while the harm keeps growing, so their sum has an optimum somewhere in the middle. On these toys it lands between \(w\approx1.5\) and \(2.5\). For Stable Diffusion on real prompts the shipped default is 7.5. The number depends on how far apart the classes are, how curved the manifold is and how bad the network’s errors are, but the shape of the trade-off doesn’t.

So CFG’s scores aren’t the noised scores of any one distribution, and it doesn’t sample the distribution it appears to target. In the SDE limit it’s a predictor-corrector that keeps pushing toward “more like the prompt than anything else”, and that push helps right up until it doesn’t.

What these toys can’t tell you

Everything here lives in two dimensions with exact scores, and dimension matters. Lehman Pavasovic et al. (2025) find a “blessing of dimensionality”: in their high-dimensional analysis, CFG’s distortions of the target shrink as dimension grows. Ventura et al. (2026) add a caveat, showing the distortions persist when the number of classes grows exponentially with dimension, which looks a lot more like open-ended text prompts. So I’d read numbers like KL 2.77, or a mean overshoot of 2.15 against 1.18, as illustrations of a mechanism. They predict nothing quantitative about a 64×64×4 latent, and this is the part of the argument I’m least sure transfers. Two other simplifications are worth knowing about. The noise process is variance-exploding, whereas Stable Diffusion 1.x and XL use variance-preserving schedules and newer models use flow matching (VP and VE are rescalings of each other, so the mechanism carries over; I haven’t checked flow matching), and the “weak model” has the simplest error structure I could write down.

What people are doing about the harm

Most of the recent work on guidance goes after one specific item on the harm list. For oversaturation and norm blow-up there’s CFG rescale (Lin et al., 2023), which rescales the guided prediction toward the conditional prediction’s standard deviation (blended back in with a factor \(\phi \approx 0.7\)) and so damps the high-norm drift from the clean-image section. APG (Sadat et al., 2024) splits the guidance update into a component parallel to the conditional prediction, which is the one that oversaturates, and an orthogonal one, which improves quality, then turns the parallel part down.

The guidance interval (Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024) targets lost diversity. It finds guidance harmful at high noise, mostly unnecessary at low noise and useful only in between, so it applies guidance only in that middle stretch (ImageNet-512 FID 1.81 → 1.40). That lines up with cell 4’s plot, where the implied clean variance goes most wrong at large \(\sigma\).

Off-manifold extrapolation is what CFG++ (Chung et al., 2024) fixes, by recasting guidance as an inverse problem so the guided step stays on the manifold, and Cai et al. (2026) add a training-free manifold projection for flow-matching models. Autoguidance (Karras et al., 2024) handles class exaggeration by replacing the unconditional model with a worse copy of the conditional one, as in cell 8. Moufad et al. (2025) take the most direct route of all. They show CFG isn’t a valid diffusion model because it drops a Rényi-divergence term that acts as a repulsive force, and they propose a Gibbs-like sampler that starts from a sample drawn without CFG and refines it toward the tilted target while preserving diversity.

Optional: try it on Stable Diffusion

If you have a GPU, the cell below shows the same mechanism on a real model. You’ll need CUDA, the diffusers stack and a one-time download of about 2.7 GB of half-precision Stable Diffusion v1.5 weights (from the stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5 mirror of the original release). It renders one prompt at \(w\in\{1, 3, 7.5, 20\}\) from the same starting noise, so the guidance weight is the only thing that changes from image to image. diffusers’ guidance_scale is exactly our \(w\).

# Optional and NOT part of the CPU build. Needs a CUDA GPU and `pip install torch diffusers transformers accelerate`;
# the first run downloads ~2.7 GB of half-precision Stable Diffusion v1.5 weights. Flip RUN_SD to True to render the sweep.
import importlib.util

RUN_SD = False
PROMPT_TEXT = "a golden retriever in a sunlit park"
SD_SCALES = [1.0, 3.0, 7.5, 20.0]          # diffusers' guidance_scale is exactly our w (1 = plain conditional)
stack_ready = all(importlib.util.find_spec(m) is not None for m in ("torch", "diffusers"))

if not (RUN_SD and stack_ready):
    print(f"Skipped (RUN_SD={RUN_SD}, diffusers installed={stack_ready}). On a GPU machine set RUN_SD = True to render w = {SD_SCALES}.")
else:
    import torch
    from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline

    pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained("stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5", torch_dtype=torch.float16, variant="fp16").to("cuda")
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3.9))
    for ax, w in zip(axes, SD_SCALES):
        generator = torch.Generator("cuda").manual_seed(SEED)   # identical starting noise for every w
        image = pipe(PROMPT_TEXT, guidance_scale=w, num_inference_steps=30, generator=generator).images[0]
        ax.imshow(image); ax.set_title(f"w = {w:g}"); ax.axis("off")
    plt.show()

Skipped (RUN_SD=False, diffusers installed=False). On a GPU machine set RUN_SD = True to render w = [1.0, 3.0, 7.5, 20.0].

In the CPU build this cell is switched off, which is why it prints “Skipped”. With RUN_SD = True on a GPU you get the 1×4 grid. Each image maps back onto one of the toys. At \(w=1\) you’re sampling \(p(x\mid c)\) from an imperfect network, so expect the hedged, washed-out look of cell 8’s weak model at \(w=1\). At 3 and 7.5 the boundary repulsion and error correction from cells 3, 7 and 8 are doing their job. At 20 you’re out on the long climb of cell 7’s harm curve, extrapolating off the manifold into high-norm pixel values that show up as oversaturated colour.

Further reading

  • Ho & Salimans (2022), Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance: the original method, short and readable. Mind the \((1+w)\) convention.
  • Bradley & Nakkiran (2024), Classifier-Free Guidance is a Predictor-Corrector: the proof that CFG doesn’t sample the gamma-powered distribution, and what it does instead.
  • Chidambaram et al. (2024), What does guidance do? A fine-grained analysis in a simple setting: the mixture analysis behind the rim pile-up in cell 5.
  • Karras et al. (2024), Guiding a Diffusion Model with a Bad Version of Itself: autoguidance, and the clearest case that guidance is partly error correction.
  • Lehman Pavasovic et al. (2025), Classifier-Free Guidance: From High-Dimensional Analysis to Generalized Guidance Forms and Ventura et al. (2026), Emergence of Distortions in High-Dimensional Guided Diffusion Models: what changes once you leave two dimensions.
  • Dieleman (2022), Guidance: a cheat code for diffusion models: a friendly tour of classifier and classifier-free guidance.
  • For background, Song et al. (2020) on the SDE and probability-flow framework, Karras et al. (2022) for the noise schedule and Heun sampler used in the code, and Fan et al. (2025), CFG-Zero* for a fix specific to flow matching.
entry.summary: Why the mathematically correct guidance setting makes the worst images, why classifier-free guidance misses the distribution it seems to target, and where exact toy models show it helping and hurting.

entry.title: Decoders Cost More Than Encoders. So Why Is Almost Every LLM a Decoder?

link.title: Decoders Cost More Than Encoders. So Why Is Almost Every LLM a Decoder?

entry.content:
Give BERT a 512-token document and it reads the whole thing in one forward pass. That’s all it does. A decoder-only LLM reads it the same way. Then it starts writing, and every token it outputs costs another full forward pass, hundreds or thousands of them in a row.

That makes decoders the expensive kind of transformer, and yet almost every frontier model of the last few years is one. I wanted to understand both halves of that properly, where the extra cost comes from and why the industry chose to pay it.

It helps to pin down what “costlier” means first. An encoder can’t generate text at all, so you can’t race the two on the same job, but you can compare cost per token. An encoder, like a decoder reading your prompt, pays for its input tokens in one parallel pass, whereas a decoder pays for each generated token with a forward pass of its own. That per-generated-token price is where the gap comes from.

The first half of the post ranks the four reasons that price is high, and the second ranks the five reasons the industry pays it anyway. Where I could, I’ve given each idea an intuition, a picture, a formula and some runnable code; a few only got three of the four.

Part 1: Why decoders cost more than encoders

One model, two modes: prefill and decode

A decoder-only model works in two modes, and only one of them is expensive.

Prefill is the reading phase. All \(L\) prompt tokens go through each layer together, so every weight matrix multiplies an \(L \times d\) activation matrix in one matrix-matrix product (a GEMM). That’s an encoder’s forward pass, give or take the causal mask. On the way through, prefill writes each prompt token’s keys and values into the KV cache, and at the end it samples the first output token. The time all that takes is the time to first token, or TTFT.

Decode is everything that follows. Each step sends one new token per request through the entire network, reads back the cached keys and values of every earlier token, and samples one more. The weights now multiply a single \(1 \times d\) vector per request, a matrix-vector product (GEMV). The gap between consecutive output tokens is the inter-token latency (ITL), and its average over a response is the time per output token (TPOT). Serving engines such as vLLM schedule the two phases differently, for the reasons in the rest of Part 1.

I picture a scribe who has to carry a whole reference shelf to the desk before writing anything. For prefill they make one trip and copy out a full page. For decode they haul the same shelf back and forth for every word, so the walking sets the pace and the writing hardly registers. The shelf is the weights, and the walking is memory traffic.

1. The GPU spends decode waiting on memory

During decode the GPU mostly waits. Its arithmetic units sit idle while data arrives from memory, and the roofline model (Williams, Waterman and Patterson, CACM 2009) shows why more cleanly than anything else I know.

Every kernel has an arithmetic intensity, the floating-point work it does for each byte it moves between HBM (the GPU’s large main memory) and the on-chip SRAM where the arithmetic happens:

\[I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}}\]

A GPU has two ceilings, peak compute in FLOP/s and HBM bandwidth in bytes/s, and a kernel runs at \(\min(\text{peak FLOP/s},\ I \times \text{bandwidth})\). On log-log axes that gives the roofline, a slope that rises with \(I\) while you’re bandwidth-bound and flattens into a roof once you’re compute-bound. The corner, peak FLOP/s divided by bandwidth, is called the ridge point. An H100 SXM moves 3.35 TB/s and does about 989 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 (NVIDIA quotes 1,979 with sparsity, and dense is half that), so its ridge sits near 295 FLOPs per byte. Any kernel to the left of that leaves tensor cores waiting.

Take a single linear layer \(Y = XW\) with \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) in BF16 and feed it \(T\) token vectors stacked in \(X\). It does \(2Td^2\) FLOPs (one multiply and one add per weight per token) and moves \(2d^2\) bytes of weights plus \(4Td\) bytes of activations, so

\[I = \frac{2Td^2}{2d^2 + 4Td} = \frac{T}{1 + 2T/d}\]

The \(T\) in the numerator counts the tokens that share one read of the weights. The \(2T/d\) in the denominator is activation traffic, which only starts to matter as \(T\) approaches \(d\), and so when \(T \ll d\) you get \(I \approx T\). In words, arithmetic intensity is roughly the number of tokens you process per trip to memory.

Most of Part 1 follows from that approximation. An encoder pass or a prefill has \(T = B \times L\) (batch size times sequence length), easily thousands of tokens. A decode step has \(L = 1\), which makes \(T = B\), nothing more than the batch size, and puts decode far down the slope while prefill sits up on the roof.

def linear_intensity(T: int, d: int, bytes_per_el: int = 2) -> float:
    """FLOPs per byte of HBM traffic for Y = X @ W with X: (T, d) and W: (d, d)."""
    flops = 2 * T * d * d                         # one multiply + one add per weight per token
    traffic = bytes_per_el * (d * d + 2 * T * d)  # read W once, read X, write Y
    return flops / traffic

def attainable_flops(I: float) -> float:
    """Roofline: you get the lower of the compute roof and the bandwidth slope."""
    return min(H100_FLOPS, I * H100_BW)

2. The KV cache caps your batch

If decode is starved because \(T = B\) is small, the natural fix is to batch more requests and push \(B\) up toward the ridge. The KV cache blocks that in two separate ways.

Without a cache, producing token \(t\) would mean recomputing keys and values for all \(t - 1\) earlier tokens at every step. So a decoder keeps them. It stores each token’s K and V vectors in every layer, appends one entry per step, and holds a separate cache for each request, since user A’s cache is no use to user B. The total size is

\[\begin{aligned} \text{KV bytes} = {} & 2 \times n_\text{layers} \times n_\text{kv heads} \times d_\text{head} \\ & \times L_\text{ctx} \times B \times \text{bytes per element} \end{aligned}\]

where the 2 counts one K and one V. \(n_\text{kv heads}\) is the number of key/value heads, which grouped-query attention (GQA, Ainslie et al., 2023) makes smaller than the number of query heads. \(L_\text{ctx}\) is how many tokens a request holds, and \(B\) is how many requests run at once. All the factors are linear, so the cache grows like a staircase, one step per user per generated token, stacked on a fixed slab of weights until it reaches the top of GPU memory.

The first problem is plain capacity. kv_bytes_per_token evaluates the formula for our 70B under three attention schemes: ordinary multi-head attention (MHA, 64 KV heads), GQA (8 KV heads), and the multi-head latent attention (MLA) from DeepSeek-V2. MLA caches one compressed 512-dimensional latent and one 64-dimensional rotary key per layer instead of per-head K and V. The MLA row is hypothetical; I kept the same 80 layers so that only the cache shape changes.

    """Bytes cached per token across every layer (the 2 is one K vector + one V vector)."""
    return 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * d_head * bytes_per_el

New requests are admitted and finished ones retired at every decode step instead of after a whole batch drains, which keeps \(B\) close to the memory cap.

The second problem survives even unlimited memory. Attention doesn’t batch. The linear layers share one set of weights across the whole batch, and that sharing is the only reason batching helps them. Attention reads each request’s own cache, so there is nothing to share. For every cached token, each KV head means reading its K and V (\(4 d_\text{head}\) bytes in BF16) to compute one dot product and one weighted sum (\(4 d_\text{head}\) FLOPs per query head). With MHA that’s about 1 FLOP per byte. GQA lets \(g = n_\text{q heads} / n_\text{kv heads}\) query heads reuse each KV head, which raises that to

\[I_\text{attn} \approx g\]

For our 70B that’s 8. It’s better than 1, but still about 37× short of the ridge, and batch size doesn’t change it. At long enough contexts these cache reads cost more bandwidth than the weight reads, as the next section shows.

3. You can’t parallelize time

Token \(y_t\) is sampled conditioned on \(y_1, \dots, y_{t-1}\), which means \(N\) tokens need \(N\) forward passes in strict order, and no amount of hardware can run them side by side. Each pass also has to stream at least the weights and the active KV cache out of HBM. Together those two facts put a floor under each user’s latency:

\[\text{TPOT}_\text{min} \approx \frac{\text{weight bytes} + \text{active KV bytes}}{\text{aggregate HBM bandwidth}}\]

The denominator is one GPU’s bandwidth times the number of GPUs the model is split across, and end-to-end latency is the TTFT plus all the inter-token gaps. Serving systems also track goodput. It counts throughput only over requests that met their latency target, because a batch that finishes quickly overall but misses its TPOT budget doesn’t help someone waiting in a chat window.

decode_step_seconds in the next cell takes the slower of memory time and compute time (I approximate compute as 2 FLOPs per parameter per token and ignore attention FLOPs), then sweeps the batch size to find where compute takes over.

def decode_step_seconds(B: int, ctx: int, n_gpus: int, weight_bytes: float, kv_per_tok: float) -> float:
    """One decode step for B users: limited by HBM traffic or by compute, whichever is slower."""
    traffic = weight_bytes + B * ctx * kv_per_tok  # every step reads all weights + every user's KV cache
    flops = 2 * MODEL["params"] * B                # ~2 FLOPs per parameter per token (attention FLOPs ignored)
    return max(traffic / (n_gpus * H100_BW), flops / (n_gpus * H100_FLOPS))

4. Cross-attention, if you kept the encoder

The smallest cost applies only to the classic encoder-decoder design used by the original Transformer, T5 and BART. Their decoder blocks have three sublayers rather than two: masked self-attention, then cross-attention (queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder’s output), then the FFN. Cross-attention brings its own \(W_Q\), \(W_K\), \(W_V\) and \(W_O\), four more \(d \times d\) matrices. An encoder block has about \(12d^2\) parameters (\(4d^2\) in attention and \(8d^2\) in an FFN with a \(4d\) hidden layer), so this decoder block comes to about \(16d^2\), roughly 33% more parameters and FLOPs.

It ranks last because decoder-only models dropped cross-attention altogether. A GPT- or Llama-style block is an encoder block with a causal mask and the same parameter count. For the models people deploy today, the whole cost gap comes from the inference mechanics in the three sections above.

Part 2: Why the industry prefers decoder-only models anyway

Part 1 adds up to a per-token tax made of low arithmetic intensity, a cache that limits the batch, and a latency floor that can’t be parallelized away. The five reasons below, biggest first, explain why the industry pays it.

1. One model for every task

Next-token prediction turns almost every language task into the same shape, text in and text out. A classifier becomes a model that generates a label and an extractor becomes one that generates JSON, while translation, summarization, coding, multi-step reasoning and tool calls are all a matter of generating the right continuation. One model behind one serving stack covers all of it.

I think this economic argument is the one that actually settles the question. Paying more per generated token for a single generalist is cheaper than building and running hundreds of task-specific encoders, each with its own labelled data, fine-tuning run, alignment, evaluation suite and deployment. Post-training (instruction tuning, RLHF, RL on verifiable rewards) is done once and reaches every downstream task through the prompt.

The research supports the zero-shot half of this argument, with one condition. Wang et al. (2022) compared architectures and pretraining objectives at scale and found that straight after unsupervised pretraining, causal decoder-only models trained autoregressively had the best zero-shot generalization. After multitask finetuning, non-causal models trained with masked language modelling came out ahead. Industry mostly operates in the first setting, with one model asked to do things nobody fine-tuned it for, steered in context and improved by general-purpose post-training rather than curated multitask mixtures.

2. Every token is a training example

At frontier pretraining budgets you want each FLOP to teach the model as much as possible, and the two objectives differ a lot on that measure.

BERT’s masked language modelling (MLM) hides 15% of the tokens and asks the model to fill them back in (Devlin et al., 2018), so the other 85% supply context but no loss. Causal language modelling (CLM) puts a loss on every position at once. With teacher forcing the input is the true sequence, and the lower-triangular mask lets position \(i\) see only tokens \(0..i\) while it predicts token \(i+1\). For a sequence of length \(L\),

\[\frac{\text{CLM loss positions}}{\text{MLM loss positions}} = \frac{L}{0.15\,L} \approx 6.7\]

Geometrically, each row of that lower-triangular mask is a separate training example, a prefix of length \(i+1\) labelled with the next token, so one forward pass trains on all \(L\) prefixes in parallel. The next cell counts loss positions under both objectives and prints the triangle.
